Its timbre belongs, with the Vietnamese đàn bầu, to the same single-string harmonic system, but the Chinese version is often heard in Jing festival ensembles and its body is sometimes made of bamboo; the Vietnamese version has been developed so that it can be plugged into amplification and has become a solo instrument. The right hand touches the string with the little finger while the other three hold a plectrum and pluck, producing a harmonic; at the same time the left hand moves the metal strip or flexible rod to change the string's tension and so the pitch. Turning it towards or away from the player raises or lowers the pitch. A beginner should first steady the right hand's touch and plucking position, then practise the left hand changing the tension in step with it, learning how the harmonic and the change of pitch work together.

It comes from the Vietnamese đàn bầu, belongs to the East Asian class of single-string instruments, and is tuned in just intonation. Its body may be a long narrow resonator, of bamboo or wood; one end of the string is fixed to the base and the other to a springy metal strip. Playing is mainly in harmonics: the right hand plucks the string with a plectrum and the left moves the metal strip to change the string's tension, raising or lowering the pitch. Jing players often perform in ensembles at festivals large and small in China, and the related Vietnamese instrument, once developed, is also used on the world-music stage.
獨弦琴又稱一弦琴，是東亞一類單弦樂器的統稱，見於中國、越南。中國資料稱其源自越南: The duxianqin, also called the one-string zither, is the general name for a class of East Asian single-string instruments, found in China and Vietnam. Chinese sources say it comes from the Vietnamese đàn bầu and describe it as a Jing instrument; it is still often played by the Jing and is common at festivals large and small. The Japanese ichigenkin arrived in the early Heian period, in the Enryaku years; the Nihon Kōki records that a man from India who had learned Chinese brought it to Japan, and in the Edo period it came in again from China. Today the duxianqin that is most widely used and that has reached the world-music stage means specifically the Vietnamese đàn bầu; it was at first an ensemble instrument, and after being developed to run through amplification it became an important solo instrument.

The string sits over a long narrow rectangular resonator, fixed at one end to the base and at the other to a springy metal strip; the source does not say what the resonator and the base are made of. The body is sometimes a large bamboo tube rather than wood; wooden bodies are more common in Vietnam.
